message.content:
Here’s a quick guide to some of the most talked‑about sushi spots you’ll find around Tokyo—ranging from world‑famous Michelin‑starred establishments to beloved local favorites that offer incredible value without breaking the bank.

| # | Restaurant | Location / Address | Why It Stands Out | Typical Price Range* | Reservation Tips |
|---|------------|--------------------|------------------|----------------------|------------------|
| **1** | **Sukiyabashi Jiro** *(now relocated)* | Formerly 5 Chome‑2‑15 Ginza, now at 7‑8‑10 Ginza 2-chōme (Ginza) | Legendary chef Jiro Ono, famed for meticulous nigiri technique; once held 3 Michelin stars. | ¥30–¥50k per person (omakase). | Must reserve months in advance via a travel agent or concierge; walk‑in rarely possible. |
| **2** | **Sushi Saito** | 9‑12‑11 Nihonbashi Honcho, Chuo Ward | Intimate 10‑seat counter, hand‑crafted pieces served as “sashimi first.” Holds 3 Michelin stars. | ¥35–¥60k per person. | Extremely hard to get a table; often booked through private connections or agencies. |
| **3** | **Kyubey** | Multiple locations: 1‑14‑18 Ginza, 1‑16‑17 Ginza, 1‑19‑20 Ginza | Classic Edo‑style sushi, long history since 1936. Known for consistent quality across its branches. | ¥25–¥40k per person. | Reservations recommended; call ahead or use their website. |
| **4** | **Sushi Yoshitake** | 1‑22‑21 Ginza, Chuo Ward | Two Michelin stars, minimalist décor, focus on seasonal ingredients. | ¥28–¥45k per person. | Reserve well in advance; they accept bookings up to 90 days prior. |
| **5** | **Umegaoka Sushino Midori** | 1‑23‑24 Ginza, Chuo Ward | Affordable yet authentic experience; offers both lunch specials and dinner omakase. | Lunch: ¥3k–¥5k; Dinner Omakase: ¥12k–¥18k. | Walk‑ins accepted during lunch hours; dinner tables fill quickly. |
| **6** | **Sushi Mizutani** | 1‑27‑26 Ginza, Chuo Ward | One Michelin star, tiny 8‑person counter, emphasis on precision cuts. | ¥20–¥32k per person. | Booking required; waitlist may exist if you’re flexible with timing. |
| **7** | **Sushi Iwa** | 1‑29‑31 Ginza, Chuo Ward | Hidden gem, only ~10 seats, celebrated for buttery toro and delicate shioyaki. | ¥25–¥38k per person. | Very short waiting lists; try calling mid‑week evenings. |
| **8** | **Sushi Dai & Sushi Daiwa** | Tsukiji Outer Market (near Toyosu station) | Iconic street stalls offering fresh catch straight off the boat. Great for breakfast/early lunch. | ¥500–¥2k per piece. | Arrive early (before 8am); line can stretch for hours. |
| **9** | **Sushi Masuda** | 1‑33‑1 Kabuki‑cho, Chuo Ward | Renowned for premium tuna selection; friendly service. | ¥20–¥36k per person. | Call ahead; they take reservations over the weekend. |
| **10** | **Sushi Kanda** | 1‑34‑1 Ginza, Chuo Ward | Three Michelin stars, extremely refined tasting menu. | ¥30–¥55k per person. | Requires booking months ahead; consider contacting a Japanese tour operator. |

\*_Prices reflect typical omakase menus; lunch specials or à la carte options vary._

### Quick Tips for Dining Out

| Tip | What it Means |
|-----|---------------|
| **Reserve Early** | Especially for Michelin‑starred venues, aim to secure a spot 2–3 months before your visit. |
| **Use Concierge Services** | Many hotels have dedicated staff who can arrange last‑minute openings or special requests. |
| **Check Online Reviews** | Sites such as *Tabelog*, *Tripadvisor*, and *Google Maps* give real‑time feedback on crowd levels and food quality. |
| **Try Local Markets** | If time is tight, head to Tsukiji/Toyosu markets for fresh sashimi and casual sushi counters. |
| **Ask About Seasonal Menus** | Some chefs change offerings weekly based on what’s freshly caught; ask the host! |
| **Be Prepared to Pay Cash** | While credit cards are increasingly accepted, smaller shops still rely on cash transactions. |

Enjoy exploring Tokyo’s vibrant sushi scene—from ultra‑luxury experiences to bustling market stalls—and savor each bite of Japan’s culinary masterpiece!
